title: Survive the Month

conceptsAssessed.concept: Distinguishing essential, optional, and context-dependent expenses.
Setting money aside before optional spending.
Balancing affordability, needs, wants, and future consequences.
Allocating limited money across essentials, saving, enjoyment, and flexibility.
Preparing for and using accessible savings for unexpected essential costs.

learningObjective: Apply budgeting, needs-versus-wants, saving, and emergency-planning skills to manage a limited amount of money for one complete month.
primaryMisconception: A successful monthly budget only needs to cover planned expenses and does not need savings or preparation for emergencies.
secondaryMisconceptions: Wants must always be removed completely from a good budget.
Borrowing is always the best solution when an unexpected expense occurs.
Saving should only happen when money remains at the end of the month.
keyTakeaway: A successful month balances needs, wants, savings, and unexpected expenses.

overview.summary: The learner manages Rs. 50,000 for one month, builds a budget, sorts needs and wants, assigns extra income, and handles an essential phone repair. Earlier choices affect later options. The final dashboard measures needs coverage, budget quality, saving behaviour, emergency readiness, debt pressure, and adaptability.

startingState.financialGoal: Finish the month with essential needs covered, manageable spending, some savings, and as little unnecessary debt as possible.

screens.title: Can Rs. 50,000 Last the Month?
screens.content: Rs. 50,000 must cover your month. Then your phone breaks. Can you protect your needs, savings, and freedom without unnecessary debt?
screens.illustration: A thirty-day calendar surrounds a Rs. 50,000 balance, essential expenses, a savings jar, and a cracked phone.

screens.title: Your Starting Position
screens.content: You receive Rs. 50,000 for the month and already have Rs. 5,000 in savings. You have no emergency fund and no debt.
screens.illustration: A dashboard showing monthly money, general savings, emergency savings, and debt.

screens.title: What the Money Must Cover
screens.content: Your month includes food, transport, mobile data, and work expenses. You also want some enjoyment and would like to finish with savings.
screens.illustration: Four essential cards and two flexible cards appear beside the monthly balance.

screens.title: A Month With Surprises
screens.content: Extra income may arrive, but an unexpected cost can appear too. Every rupee used now changes what remains later.
screens.illustration: A timeline hides event cards behind Week 2 and Week 3.

stateSummary.financialGoal: Cover needs, keep spending manageable, save something, and avoid unnecessary debt.

screens.title: What Should the Budget Do?
screens.question: Which monthly plan sounds most balanced?

options.label: Cover planned bills and spend everything else
options.feedback: This may work until an unexpected cost appears.

options.label: Cover needs, save something, and leave room for affordable wants
options.feedback: Correct. The simulation will test whether this balance survives a changing month.

options.label: Remove every want, even when affordable
options.feedback: A budget can include enjoyment when needs and future priorities remain protected.

options.label: Borrow whenever the month becomes difficult
options.feedback: Borrowing may solve an urgent problem, but it creates a later obligation.

screens.connectionToSimulation: The next four stages test whether the learner can balance essentials, enjoyment, savings, flexibility, and an emergency.

stages.title: Build the Budget
stages.situation: Your Rs. 50,000 must last the month. Food, transport, mobile data, and work expenses have minimum costs. You also decide how much to save, spend on enjoyment, or leave as a flexible buffer.
stages.objective: Cover every essential minimum without exceeding Rs. 50,000.

choices.label: Valid balanced budget
choices.immediateFeedback: Needs are covered, some money is saved, and enjoyment or flexibility remains.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The month begins with essential categories funded.
choices.laterConsequence: Savings, entertainment money, and the buffer may help with the repair.

choices.label: Valid budget with no entertainment
choices.immediateFeedback: The maths works, but the plan may feel restrictive.
choices.laterConsequence: More money may remain for savings or emergencies.

choices.label: Essential category below minimum
choices.immediateFeedback: One essential expense is not covered.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The plan may not last the month.
choices.laterConsequence: An essential payment may be missed.

choices.label: Budget above Rs. 50,000
choices.immediateFeedback: The plan uses more money than is available.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Cover every essential minimum, save something, and use remaining money for affordable enjoyment or a buffer.
reasonableAlternatives: A no-entertainment budget may be reasonable when the learner prefers faster saving.
A smaller saving amount may be reasonable when essential costs are higher.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: More saving increases protection but leaves less money for current enjoyment.

validation.method: Check essential minimums, total allocations, non-negative values, and remaining balance.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Cover every essential minimum and keep the total at or below Rs. 50,000.
validation.retryBehaviour: Keep valid values and highlight only the amount causing the error.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use labelled plus and minus buttons.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Adjust each category and listen to the remaining balance.

stateSummary.title: Budget Locked

changedValues.reason: Savings are set aside before optional spending.

stateSummary.learningMessage: A realistic budget protects needs, future priorities, and flexibility.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Decide which everyday expenses should be protected first.

stages.title: Need, Want, or Depends?
stages.situation: Your budget is set, but real purchases do not always arrive with clear labels. Sort six expenses before deciding what should be protected when money becomes tight.
stages.objective: Classify every expense by its purpose and context.

sortableItems.label: New gaming headphones
sortableItems.explanation: Usually optional when working audio is available.

sortableItems.label: Restaurant meal
sortableItems.explanation: Its role depends on circumstances and alternatives.

sortableItems.label: Internet package
sortableItems.explanation: May be essential for work or optional as an upgrade.

sortableItems.label: Premium shoes when usable shoes are available

config.ambiguityExplanation: Judge the expense by its purpose, alternatives, and consequences.

choices.label: Complete all six classifications
choices.immediateFeedback: You separated clear needs and wants while recognising context-dependent expenses.
choices.laterConsequence: The emergency stage can protect needs before flexible spending.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Protect health, safety, work, and basic functioning. Treat upgrades as flexible and review context-dependent expenses.
reasonableAlternatives: A restaurant meal may become necessary when no practical alternative exists.
Internet may be essential for work while a premium upgrade is optional.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Calling every expense a need removes flexibility; calling every expense a want may leave needs unprotected.

validation.method: Compare all six placements with their categories.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Review the purpose of the item and whether an alternative exists.
validation.retryBehaviour: Keep correct items and retry only incorrect placements.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present one item at a time with three labelled buttons.

stateSummary.title: Priorities Identified
stateSummary.learningMessage: Needs should be protected, wants can be managed, and some expenses depend on context.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: An extra Rs. 5,000 is about to arrive.

stages.title: Saving First
stages.situation: You earn an unexpected Rs. 5,000 from a small freelance task. Your savings, emergency fund, buffer, and entertainment budget carry forward.
stages.objective: Decide how the extra income should support the rest of the month.

startingNode.question: What should the extra Rs. 5,000 do?

followUpNode.question: How might this affect a surprise later?

choices.label: Save all of it for emergencies
choices.immediateFeedback: The full Rs. 5,000 moves into the emergency fund.
choices.laterConsequence: The repair may require less savings or debt.

choices.label: Spend all of it on a want
choices.immediateFeedback: The extra income provides immediate enjoyment.
choices.shortTermConsequence: No additional emergency protection is created.
choices.laterConsequence: The repair may place more pressure on savings or debt.

choices.label: Save Rs. 3,000 and spend Rs. 2,000
choices.immediateFeedback: Part of the income is protected and part supports enjoyment.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The emergency fund increases by Rs. 3,000.
choices.laterConsequence: The repair still needs another funding source.

choices.label: Keep all Rs. 5,000 available as a buffer
choices.laterConsequence: The money can help with the repair but is not formally protected.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Saving all is generally strongest because the learner begins with no emergency fund.
reasonableAlternatives: Saving part and spending part is reasonable when existing savings are strong.
Keeping the money available is reasonable when a necessary cost is expected soon.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: More enjoyment now means less protection later.

validation.method: Accept one choice and apply its state changes.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: No choice is invalid. Review the trade-off.

accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Choose how to use the extra income and listen to the balance changes.

stateSummary.title: Extra Income Assigned

changedValues.reason: The decision changes the resources available later.

stateSummary.learningMessage: Saving first turns unexpected income into future choices.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: An essential repair will test your plan.

stages.title: The Phone Emergency
stages.situation: Your phone stops working. The Rs. 8,000 repair is essential for work and communication. The resources available depend on earlier choices.
stages.objective: Predict which response best protects needs, then choose how to pay.

prediction.question: Which approach is most likely to protect essential needs and limit new debt?

options.label: Use prepared emergency money and accessible savings
Borrow immediately without checking resources
Skip another essential payment
Ignore the repair

prediction.explanation: Prepared savings and flexible categories can reduce pressure, but the strongest choice depends on available balances.

choices.label: Use emergency money first, then accessible savings
choices.immediateFeedback: The repair is paid from resources prepared earlier.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The phone is repaired without missing another need.

choices.label: Borrow Rs. 8,000
choices.immediateFeedback: The repair is completed, but debt is created.

choices.label: Skip transport payments
choices.immediateFeedback: The repair is paid, but an essential obligation is left uncovered.
choices.laterConsequence: The dashboard records a missed need.

choices.label: Reduce optional spending and use savings for the rest
choices.immediateFeedback: Flexible money is redirected to the repair.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The phone can be repaired without debt when enough resources exist.
choices.laterConsequence: The month includes less enjoyment and lower savings.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Use emergency savings first when available, then accessible savings or buffer.
reasonableAlternatives: Reducing optional spending is strong when emergency savings are insufficient.
Borrowing may be reasonable when the repair is essential and accessible resources are insufficient.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Using savings reduces future protection; borrowing preserves cash but creates repayment pressure.

validation.method: Confirm cash-funded sources total Rs. 8,000 or apply the borrowing or missed-obligation result.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Those sources do not total Rs. 8,000.
validation.retryBehaviour: Risky valid choices may continue. Insufficient cash choices must be revised.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use labelled choice buttons and announce each source used.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Choose a repair response and listen to updated savings, debt, and needs.

stateSummary.title: The Month's Final Test

changedValues.reason: The repair is paid using the selected sources.
The emergency response changes the final position.

stateSummary.learningMessage: Earlier saving and flexible spending choices determine which emergency responses are available.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: A larger saving allocation creates more non-debt repair options.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Shows why saving belongs inside the budget.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: Unspent optional money can be redirected to the repair.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Shows that wants are flexible rather than automatically irresponsible.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: Saving all extra income covers most of the repair.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Connects saving first with emergency readiness.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: Spending all extra income leaves no new emergency protection.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Shows the delayed trade-off of immediate spending.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: The dashboard shows an Rs. 8,000 obligation.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Shows that borrowing changes the ending position.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: Essential needs are marked as needing attention.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Shows that shifting money away from one need creates another problem.

midMissionCheckpoint.title: Halfway Through the Month

positiveDecisionFeedbackRules.message: You protected your essential needs and increased savings.
Your essential monthly costs are covered.

emergingRiskFeedbackRules.message: You have little protection if an unexpected expense appears.
Your plan may feel restrictive if no room remains for enjoyment.
A large surprise could place pressure on your savings.

midMissionCheckpoint.reflectionQuestion: Continue with this plan, or review the budget before the next event?

finalChallenge.title: The Phone Repair
finalChallenge.situation: In Week 3, the learner must cover an essential Rs. 8,000 repair using resources created by earlier budgeting and saving decisions.
finalChallenge.recommendedReasoning: Use prepared emergency money when available. Reducing optional spending is also reasonable. Borrowing may be necessary when accessible resources are insufficient, but skipping another essential payment shifts the problem.

debrief.title: A Budget Is More Than Planned Bills
debrief.content: You managed one month by balancing essential costs, savings, enjoyment, extra income, and an unexpected repair. A successful budget also creates flexibility when real life changes. Saving before optional spending can reduce pressure later, while affordable wants may still fit. Borrowing can help when an essential cost cannot otherwise be covered, but it creates future obligations. The strongest response depends on the resources and priorities already in place.
debrief.simpleSummary: Balance needs, wants, savings, and flexibility before the surprise arrives.
debrief.illustration: Needs, savings, flexibility, and thoughtful decisions form a shield around the monthly calendar.

dimensions.label: Budget Quality
positiveRules: 25 points for essentials, saving, affordability, and enjoyment or a buffer.
20 points for essentials and saving with no optional spending.
15 points for essentials with no saving.
deductions: Invalid budgets must be revised before continuing.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: A strong budget protects needs and remains realistic.

dimensions.label: Needs and Wants Judgement
positiveRules: Fewer than three earns 4 after completion.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Good decisions recognise needs, wants, and context.

dimensions.label: Saving Behaviour
deductions: Up to four points for no Stage 1 saving allocation.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Saving before optional spending creates more future choices.

dimensions.label: Emergency Response
positiveRules: Reduce optional spending and use savings: 22.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: The strongest response protects needs while limiting new pressure.

dimensions.label: Financial Adaptability
positiveRules: Choice fits earlier resources and no need is missed: 10.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Adaptability means changing the plan without losing sight of needs.

performanceLevels.label: Financially Vulnerable
performanceLevels.description: The month ended with uncovered needs, little preparation, or heavy debt pressure.

performanceLevels.label: Building Stability
performanceLevels.description: Several decisions worked, but saving, prioritisation, or emergency preparation need attention.

performanceLevels.label: Financially Prepared
performanceLevels.description: Most needs, savings, enjoyment, and emergency trade-offs were balanced effectively.

performanceLevels.label: Strong Financial Habits
performanceLevels.description: The learner made consistent and adaptable decisions. This does not guarantee future financial success.

strengthRules.message: You built a budget that protected essential costs and future priorities.
You used extra income to strengthen savings or flexibility.
You handled the phone repair without sacrificing another essential need.
You recognised essential, optional, and context-dependent expenses.

improvementRules.message: A small emergency buffer earlier would have created more options.
The repair created debt. Review whether savings or flexible spending could reduce future borrowing.
An essential payment was missed. Protecting needs first would make the plan more stable.
Saving part of the extra income could reduce later pressure.

tradeoffRules.message: You kept enjoyment without losing essential coverage. The trade-off was slower saving.
You prioritised saving strongly. The trade-off was a more restrictive month.
Borrowing solved the repair but created a repayment obligation.

personalisedFeedbackRules.practicalPrinciple: Cover needs, save something early, and keep enough flexibility to handle a surprise.

questions.question: Which monthly plan uses budgeting and emergency preparation together?

options.label: Cover planned bills and spend every remaining rupee
options.feedback: This leaves no protection for surprises.

options.label: Cover needs, save early, and include affordable wants
options.feedback: Correct. The plan balances current life with preparation.

options.label: Reduce food spending to increase savings
options.feedback: Saving should not make essential needs unaffordable.

options.label: Borrow whenever anything unexpected happens
options.feedback: Borrowing may help but creates a future obligation.

questions.correctExplanation: A balanced plan covers needs, saves before optional spending, and allows affordable enjoyment.
questions.misconceptionTested: A budget only needs to cover planned expenses.

questions.question: Why should a monthly budget include savings before the month ends?

options.label: Every month guarantees an emergency
options.feedback: An emergency is not guaranteed, but preparation creates options.

options.label: Saving early protects money from being fully spent
options.feedback: Correct. Saving becomes planned instead of depending on leftovers.

options.label: Wants are always irresponsible
options.feedback: Affordable wants may fit after needs and future priorities.

options.label: Savings remove the need for a budget
options.feedback: Savings work best as part of a complete budget.

questions.correctExplanation: Saving first turns saving into a planned action.
questions.misconceptionTested: Saving should only happen at the end of the month.

questions.question: A Rs. 6,000 medical cost appears. You have Rs. 3,000 emergency savings, Rs. 4,000 optional money, and no debt. What is the strongest response?

options.label: Skip transport and keep the optional money
options.feedback: This leaves another essential need uncovered.

options.label: Use emergency savings and reduce optional spending
options.feedback: Correct. This uses prepared savings and a flexible category.

options.label: Borrow the full amount immediately
options.feedback: Accessible resources can cover the cost without debt.

options.label: Ignore the cost because it was not budgeted
options.feedback: An essential unexpected cost still needs a response.

questions.correctExplanation: The response combines emergency preparation and flexible spending without missing a need.
questions.misconceptionTested: Borrowing is always the best emergency solution.

realLifeChallenge.title: Plan for One Surprise
realLifeChallenge.instruction: Write one fictional weekly expense, label it Need, Want, or Depends, and note one free adjustment you could make if an emergency appeared. Do not share private financial information or move money.

No claims that markets always recover
Scoring rewards decision quality rather than luck
Enjoyable spending is not automatically irresponsible
Language matches the target reading level
Final dashboard matches the simulation outcomes
